newsitem.title: USA: Next Congress poised to pass more environmental bills.
newsitem.headline: Next Congress poised to pass more environmental bills.

text.p: The 104th Congress, once denounced by critics as the most anti-environment ever, passed in its final months a flurry of bills supported by greens.
And that may continue in the 105th if voters prod more lawmakers to the political centre, where they are more able to make compromises necessary to pass bills, some analysts said.
"It seems to me that people on the extremes, on the fringes who don't adjust, a lot of them may not be re-elected," said Don Gray of the Environmental and Energy Study Institute think tank.

"I think what you'll see is some people, as a part of their re-election strategy, will start to take a softer line on the environment, and I think that certainly increases the chance (of legislation passing)," Gray said.

"This Congress produced a lot of long-sought environmental reforms and that should be the pattern in the coming Congress rather than getting caught up in a lot of ideological battles," said David Goldstin, an aide to moderate Republican Representative Sherwood Boehlert of New York.

Environmental groups hope to be in a stronger position next year on major bills such as reauthorizing laws for clean water, endangered species and Superfund toxic waste cleanups. But they said their strength hinges on how potent an issue the environment turns out to be in next month's elections.

"What we saw right up to the end was those forces that have been promoting what we consider to be fundamental weakenings of environmental protection continue to have that agenda, and the question is how much leverage will they have," said Greg Wetstone of the Natural Resources Defence Council.

Industry groups said they were largely blocked in getting changes to let them do business without unnecessary government interference because environmentalists and the Clinton administration branded their legislation as extremist.

"If you look at most of the actual proposals that were considered, few of them were really that radical in nature," said Richard Siebert, National Association of Manufacturers' vice president for resources, environment and regulation.

Siebert said industry efforts now may focus more on getting admininistrative changes at the Environmental Protection Agency and other regulatory agencies and trying to influence the outcome of specific regulations.

The Republican-led 104th -- largely stymied by President Bill Clinton's veto threats and by Senate moderates -- passed few of the bills pushed by industry to curb environmental rules and increase access to timber, minerals and other resources on federal lands.

After being hammered in public opinion polls that said voters wanted strong rules against polluters, Republicans shifted gears to pass several significant environmental bills that had been stalled for years.
"We passed this stuff, get no credit, and they still call us the most extreme Congress," complained a Republican aide to the House Commerce Committee.
Laws were enacted for new safe drinking water protections, food safety and pesticide reforms and stronger restrictions against overfishing and wasting marine resources.
Republicans said they would have passed more but the Clinton administration successfully portrayed many bills -- and Republican backers -- as pandering to polluters.
